artifact.hint: Leonardo da Vinci's portrait vanished from the Louvre with its provenance card, shipping sleeve, and conservation notes.

pattern.label: Renaissance provenance route
pattern.summary: The thief is laundering the painting through places tied to Renaissance art, museum catalogues, and old European collection routes.

route.learningGoal: Understand the Mona Lisa as a Louvre icon and a French royal-to-national museum object.
route.thiefClaim: The Louvre is only the final holder, so its claim is shallow.
route.truthComplication: French collection history is part of the painting's biography, even though Leonardo painted it in Italy.

route.learningGoal: Connect Leonardo, Renaissance workshop culture, and Florence to the portrait's creation context.
route.thiefClaim: Florence proves the painting has one rightful cultural home.
route.truthComplication: Origin explains creation, but not the whole later life of the object.

route.learningGoal: Show how Leonardo's last years in France and French royal collecting became part of the painting's life story.
route.thiefClaim: The move into French royal hands was just the first mistake in the provenance chain.
route.truthComplication: Court transfer changed the object's history permanently; later custody is not noise to erase.

route.learningGoal: Use restoration and old-master records to compare Renaissance and northern European collection evidence.
route.thiefClaim: Technical archives can be edited until the route looks certain.
route.truthComplication: Conservation evidence can clarify movement, but it cannot rewrite authorship or ownership.

route.learningGoal: Expose a false museum-transfer file built from real European collection patterns.
route.thiefClaim: A forged Prado exchange record can make the return route look official.
route.truthComplication: Museum paperwork is evidence only when it fits the whole provenance chain.

clues.title: Baggage direction
clues.text: A private crate left Paris for a European country southeast of the Louvre. The handler remembered a destination tied to Leonardo, not to a modern auction house.

clues.title: Florence shelf mark
clues.text: The Louvre register is missing a Florence loan sleeve. Its old shelf mark names a Renaissance workshop file, not a Paris exhibition file.

clues.title: Trade packing
clues.text: The crate padding used a wine merchant's sleeve and clothing-house inventory paper. It looks like cover cargo from a country known for wine and fashion exports.

clues.title: Romance-language permit
clues.text: The permit translation stayed inside the Romance-language corridor, but the seal did not match France, Spain, or Portugal. ACME flags Italy as the cleanest fit.

clues.title: Conservator request
clues.text: A guest asked for a late train to a city with portrait conservation labs and Renaissance archives. The city name was not written down, but the question sounded like Florence.

followups.text: Back in Paris, the Louvre archivist confirms the missing shelf mark belonged to a Florence loan file, not a Paris exhibition file.

clues.title: French court note
clues.text: The Uffizi transfer note says the portrait's track leaves Tuscany only after Leonardo's final years, toward a French royal residence in the Loire Valley.

clues.title: Loire route
clues.text: The courier route bends northwest from Florence toward a smaller French stop rather than a capital museum office.

clues.title: Clos Lucé booking
clues.text: A guest asked for a driver to the house where Leonardo spent his final years under French patronage. The clerk wrote down Amboise.

clues.title: French royal seal
clues.text: The transit seal is French and references an old royal inventory series, not an Italian restoration office.

clues.title: Dutch restoration note
clues.text: A copied French court inventory page was annotated by Dutch restorers and old-master dealers in Amsterdam.

clues.title: Canal workshop invoice
clues.text: The packing invoice includes machinery and chemical supplies tied to a conservation workshop in the Low Countries.

clues.title: Low-country transfer
clues.text: The crate left France for a low-lying northern country with canals, still inside Europe and well away from royal residences.

clues.title: Canal booking
clues.text: The thief asked for a hotel near canals and a restoration studio, then corrected the clerk when he suggested Bruges. The booking was for Amsterdam.

clues.title: Prado cross-reference
clues.text: The Rijksmuseum restoration note points to a Spanish royal collection file. The exchange number is stamped for the Prado freight office.

clues.title: Southwest sleeve
clues.text: The cargo sleeve shows a southwest route inside Europe, toward a capital whose name starts with M.

clues.title: Mediterranean cargo relabel
clues.text: The fake cargo relabel lists wine, vehicles, and Mediterranean food shipments. It is too southern for the Low Countries and too western for Italy.

clues.title: Spanish seal
clues.text: The replacement export seal is Spanish, but the stated artwork origin is false. That contradiction is strong enough for a warrant in Madrid.

deadEnds.default: The field office found no match for the cultural pattern. At least one strong clue contradicts this destination.
deadEnds.France: The trail began in France, but the collected evidence points away from the Louvre after the theft.
deadEnds.Portugal: Portugal fits part of the Romance-language trail, but the Renaissance and export evidence do not support it.
deadEnds.Belgium: Belgium fits the Low Countries clue, but the language and canal-restoration evidence point farther north.

artifact.hint: A trilingual inscription file disappeared from the British Museum, leaving only a rubbed copy and a false customs card.

pattern.label: Ancient scripts and decipherment route
pattern.summary: The thief follows translation archives, pharaonic evidence, and places where script fragments can be turned into a false origin story.

route.learningGoal: Frame the Rosetta Stone as a British Museum object with an older Egyptian life and a modern display story.
route.thiefClaim: The current display location is irrelevant because the stone's root is elsewhere.
route.truthComplication: Current display is not origin, but it is part of how the object became globally known.

route.learningGoal: Tie the stone to the Nile Delta discovery site and the local geography that gave it its European name.
route.thiefClaim: Discovery near Rashid settles the object's true destination by itself.
route.truthComplication: Discovery location matters, but the object's later Egyptian, European, and scholarly histories still matter too.

route.learningGoal: Connect the inscription to ancient Egypt, pharaonic context, and modern Egyptian cultural identity.
route.thiefClaim: Once the stone re-enters Egyptian custody, the rest of the route becomes irrelevant.
route.truthComplication: National custody is a real chapter, but it does not erase how the object was discovered, captured, studied, and displayed.

route.learningGoal: Use translation history and ancient learning to show why the stone changed how scripts were understood.
route.thiefClaim: A translation archive can certify the thief's return narrative.
route.truthComplication: Scholarship explains meaning; it does not make forged custody records true.

route.learningGoal: Show how the stone's European decipherment story became part of its global afterlife and how the thief abuses that prestige.
route.thiefClaim: French decipherment gives Paris the authority to rewrite the final provenance.
route.truthComplication: Scholarship made the stone famous, but fame and interpretation do not create legal custody.

clues.title: Three scripts, one destination
clues.text: The empty case was dusted with a rubbing of Greek, Demotic, and hieroglyphic text. The margin note points to the Nile Delta discovery site, not another European archive.

clues.title: Decipherment shelf
clues.text: The stolen catalogue card was filed beside ancient-script research, Nile Delta maps, and a sketch labelled Rashid.

clues.title: Granodiorite invoice
clues.text: A fake stone-sample invoice moved with gold and textile paperwork. The cargo language points to a North African port town, not another London collector.

clues.title: Delta permit
clues.text: The permit is valid only for a restricted antiquities survey near Rashid. The description is forged, but the destination line is clear.

clues.title: Cairo custody line
clues.text: The Delta transfer ledger forwards every formal custody reference to Cairo's national museum files, not to a local holding room.

clues.title: Capital run
clues.text: The courier route stays within Egypt and follows the Nile corridor toward the capital rather than back to the coast.

clues.title: Museum wrapping
clues.text: The wrapping bears a Cairo antiquities registry code beneath the forged shipping number.

clues.title: National custody
clues.text: The antiquities authority confirms the next clean file in the chain is the national museum archive in Cairo.

clues.title: Alexandria translation slip
clues.text: The Cairo archive has a duplicate translation slip requested by a library on the Mediterranean coast. The signature points to Alexandria.

clues.title: Coastal hop
clues.text: The courier did not leave Egypt. The travel sleeve names a coastal research city west of Cairo.

clues.title: Library request
clues.text: A translation request arrived from a modern library built around ancient Alexandria's scholarly reputation.

clues.title: Alexandria authority
clues.text: The cultural authority confirms the duplicate translation slip was requested for Alexandria, not another Cairo archive.

clues.title: Paris correspondence
clues.text: The Alexandria correspondence points to Paris scholars who turned the stone into a European decipherment legend. The thief is leaning on that prestige.

clues.title: Mediterranean hop
clues.text: The next flight leaves the Mediterranean for a European capital where script scholarship became part of the object's fame.

clues.title: Seine scholar booking
clues.text: A scholar's alias was booked near a Paris archive, not another museum gallery or coastal library.

clues.title: French academy seal
clues.text: The forged final paperwork uses a French academic seal to make a fake decipherment-based transfer look legitimate.

deadEnds.default: The script evidence does not fit this destination. The stronger clues still point toward Egypt and its translation archives.
deadEnds.Greece: The Greek text matters, but the stone trail is not moving to Greece.
deadEnds.France: French decipherment history is tempting, but the permits and cargo records point back to Egypt.

artifact.hint: Sculpture fragments vanished from a disputed collection file, leaving a restitution memo and a marble dust trail.

pattern.label: Classical sculpture and restitution route
pattern.summary: The thief moves through classical sculpture evidence, marble source notes, and restitution claims tied to Athens.

route.learningGoal: Introduce the sculptures as a disputed collection displayed far from the building they came from.
route.thiefClaim: The London display is only a colonial interruption.
route.truthComplication: The dispute is real, but forged restitution paperwork still has to be proven false.

route.learningGoal: Connect modern restitution arguments with a museum built to interpret the Acropolis material.
route.thiefClaim: A modern origin-claim institution can authorize the whole route.
route.truthComplication: A strong cultural claim is not the same thing as permission for theft.

route.learningGoal: Tie the fragments back to the Parthenon and their architectural site context.
route.thiefClaim: The original site cancels every later chapter.
route.truthComplication: Site context is essential, but the investigation must preserve evidence instead of replacing it with a slogan.

clues.title: Athens claim file
clues.text: The stolen file references a restitution claim, Pentelic marble, and a museum below the Acropolis. It points away from London and toward Athens.

clues.title: Classical sculpture shelf
clues.text: The archive shelf is indexed under classical sculpture, democracy, and the Parthenon. ACME marks Greece as the historic match.

clues.title: Mediterranean packing
clues.text: The false packing list names olive oil and fish beside marble tools. The climate note reads Mediterranean.

clues.title: Athens letterhead
clues.text: A forged cultural-loan letter uses Greek ministry formatting and names Athens as the receiving city.

clues.title: Site alignment
clues.text: The Acropolis Museum alignment table sends the investigator up to the ancient citadel itself. The stolen fragment's edge matches a site record, not a storage room.

clues.title: Rooftop sightline
clues.text: A courier requested a room with a direct view of the Acropolis, then left before sunrise with a long crate.

clues.title: Site warrant
clues.text: The final warrant names Athens and the Acropolis site record. ACME has enough confirmation to close the fragment pattern.

deadEnds.default: The marble and restitution evidence does not fit this destination.
deadEnds.Italy: Rome fits classical history, but the specific Parthenon and Acropolis evidence points to Athens.
deadEnds.United Kingdom: The case begins in London, but every useful claim file points away from it.

artifact.hint: A Hokusai print and its maritime ledger vanished, leaving blue pigment traces and a shipping account.

pattern.label: Ukiyo-e print and maritime image route
pattern.summary: The thief follows Hokusai records, Dutch print-trade catalogues, and a final American collection ledger.

route.learningGoal: Connect Hokusai, Edo print culture, Mount Fuji imagery, and the print's Japanese context.
route.thiefClaim: The print's origin makes every later collection secondary.
route.truthComplication: The Great Wave is rooted in Japan but became globally influential through circulation.

route.learningGoal: Show how maritime trade routes and Dutch-Japanese contact opened channels through which Japanese prints could travel outward.
route.thiefClaim: The print left Japan through a single corrupt export corridor that can be reversed cleanly.
route.truthComplication: Trade routes moved objects and ideas, but they rarely form a simple reversible chain.

route.learningGoal: Show how print collecting and Dutch-Japanese cultural routes helped move Japanese images into Europe.
route.thiefClaim: European records are just contamination to be removed.
route.truthComplication: Collection routes can distort context, but they also explain how influence spread.

route.learningGoal: Trace how Japanese prints reshaped European taste, collecting, and modern art through Parisian salons and critics.
route.thiefClaim: Paris proves the image was consumed as fashion, not respected as culture.
route.truthComplication: European enthusiasm distorted context, but it also formed part of the print's modern worldwide significance.

route.learningGoal: Expose the thief's final attempt to turn a global collection history into a fake proof of improper removal.
route.thiefClaim: An American collection file proves the print wandered too far from its rightful home.
route.truthComplication: Global collecting can be unequal, but the final forged transfer still has to be disproved with evidence.

clues.title: Dejima note
clues.text: The missing ledger references a western Japanese harbor where Dutch trade paperwork once touched Japanese print routes. The margin says Nagasaki.

clues.title: Domestic westbound hop
clues.text: The first move stays inside Japan and heads west toward a port city rather than directly overseas.

clues.title: Port wrapping
clues.text: The wrapping includes harbor codes and cargo twine used by maritime traders, not by inland print sellers.

clues.title: Domestic customs stamp
clues.text: The first customs stamp is domestic and Japanese. The export stage starts later.

clues.title: Dutch print-trade entry
clues.text: The Nagasaki trade ledger points to Amsterdam and a Dutch old-master catalogue shelf that handled Japanese print records.

clues.title: Blue-paper shipment
clues.text: The wrapping included machinery paperwork and a packet marked for a canal-side print dealer.

clues.title: Westbound art freight
clues.text: The crate moved west from Tokyo to Europe, not across the Pacific. The routing label mentions a temperate maritime destination.

clues.title: Dutch customs stamp
clues.text: The customs stamp is Dutch, and the permit number matches a museum print department in Amsterdam.

clues.title: Paris salon card
clues.text: A Rijksmuseum circulation card points to Paris salons where Japanese prints changed European taste and criticism.

clues.title: Short continental hop
clues.text: The next move is a short west-southwest hop to a European capital on the Seine rather than across the Atlantic.

clues.title: Critics' index
clues.text: The critics' index is full of Paris addresses, collectors, and salon notes about Japanese prints.

clues.title: French collector seal
clues.text: The sealed packet matches a Paris collector's route rather than another Dutch museum transfer.

clues.title: Freer accession number
clues.text: The Paris correspondence contains a copied accession number for an Asian art collection in Washington, D.C., where the thief plans the final proof swap.

clues.title: Atlantic sleeve
clues.text: The next crate crossed the Atlantic toward a capital city, not a commercial art hub.

clues.title: Industrial cover manifest
clues.text: The cover manifest lists aircraft parts and electronics. It fits an American customs file better than another European stop.

clues.title: Washington catalogue
clues.text: The catalogue request names Washington, D.C. and an Asian art gallery. ACME marks the American collection ledger as the final proof point.

deadEnds.default: The print-trade ledger does not support this destination.
deadEnds.United Kingdom: The British Museum appears in print history, but this route's records move through Amsterdam first.
deadEnds.Japan: The theft begins in Japan. The ledger points outward after the first scene.

artifact.hint: The Sun Stone file was stolen from Mexico City, along with an excavation note and a cathedral-era storage reference.

pattern.label: Calendar stone and Mesoamerican provenance route
pattern.summary: The thief is not crossing borders first; the pattern hides the object inside Mexico City's own museum, temple, and excavation records.

route.learningGoal: Introduce the Sun Stone as a national museum object tied to Mexica identity and Mexico City.
route.thiefClaim: A national display still separates the stone from its sacred urban root.
route.truthComplication: The museum protects and interprets the object as part of modern national memory.

route.learningGoal: Connect the object to Tenochtitlan, Mexica sacred geography, and the archaeological center of the city.
route.thiefClaim: The temple site is the only context that matters.
route.truthComplication: The site is crucial, but the object's modern museum life is also part of its cultural biography.

route.learningGoal: Expose a false local transfer that turns valid site evidence into a forged custody claim.
route.thiefClaim: A nearby museum archive can make the local return official.
route.truthComplication: Even a local route needs proof; proximity cannot replace records.

clues.title: Temple site note
clues.text: The stolen object card names Mexica sculpture and a site-evidence file at Templo Mayor. The thief is still inside Mexico City.

clues.title: Mesoamerican bibliography
clues.text: The bibliography points to Aztec and Maya pyramids, a Mesoamerican provenance argument, and the old center of Tenochtitlan.

clues.title: Local cover manifest
clues.text: The manifest lists vehicles and electronics, but every address stays in Mexico City. There is no border-crossing customs mark.

clues.title: No export permit
clues.text: The registry confirms no legal export permit exists. The next scene is domestic and tied to the temple site.

clues.title: Museum case number
clues.text: The Templo Mayor site card matches a museum case number a few streets away. The false provenance will be filed at the Templo Mayor Museum.

clues.title: Curator's shortcut
clues.text: A visiting curator heard the courier ask for the shortest walk from the excavation site to the museum archive.

clues.title: Local warrant
clues.text: The warrant names Mexico City and the Templo Mayor Museum archive. The pattern is local, but the evidence is complete.

deadEnds.default: The Sun Stone evidence is unusually local; this lead does not support an international jump.
deadEnds.Spain: Colonial records may matter later, but the current excavation evidence stays in Mexico City.
deadEnds.Guatemala: Mesoamerican context is relevant, but the object and scene evidence both point to Mexico.
